blueprint_topic: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — fentanyl transdermal heat-exposure safety
stem: An opioid-tolerant client uses a fentanyl transdermal system for severe persistent pain. Which statement by the client requires correction?

options.A: I will keep heating pads and electric blankets away from the patch application site and the surrounding skin.
options.B: I will avoid hot tubs, saunas, hot baths, and other direct external heat while I am wearing the patch.
options.C: I can place a heating pad over the patch for breakthrough pain if I limit the heat exposure to about 15 minutes.
options.D: If I develop a high fever while wearing the patch, I will contact my healthcare provider because higher body temperature can increase fentanyl exposure.

rationale: Current fentanyl transdermal system labeling warns that direct external heat can increase fentanyl absorption and has resulted in overdose and death. Patients are instructed to avoid direct external heat sources such as heating pads, electric blankets, hot baths, saunas, and hot tubs at the application site and surrounding area. The label also warns that elevated body temperature can increase fentanyl concentrations and instructs patients with high fever to contact their healthcare provider. Therefore C requires correction because the label does not provide a safe short-duration heating-pad exception. A, B, and D reflect current labeling.
educational_objective: Teach clients using fentanyl transdermal systems to avoid direct external heat at the patch site and surrounding area and to report high fever because heat can increase fentanyl absorption and overdose risk.
source_organization: DailyMed (U.S. National Library of Medicine); Mylan Pharmaceuticals Inc.
source_document_title: Fentanyl Transdermal System CII — Prescribing Information
source_locator: Highlights and Full Prescribing Information §5.8 Risk of Increased Fentanyl Absorption with Application of External Heat: direct external heat at the application site or surrounding area may increase fentanyl absorption and has resulted in overdose and death; patients should avoid heating pads, electric blankets, heat/tanning lamps, sunbathing, hot baths, saunas, hot tubs, and heated water beds. §2.7 Administration — Avoidance of Heat repeats the external-heat restriction. §5.9 Risk of Increased Fentanyl Absorption with Elevated Body Temperature advises close monitoring for fever and instructs patients to contact their healthcare provider if high fever develops.
source_claim_supported: Direct external heat at or around a fentanyl transdermal system can increase fentanyl absorption and has caused fatal overdose; patients should avoid external heat sources and seek guidance if high fever develops.
blueprint_locator: Printed p. 38, Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies: educate clients about medications; review pertinent medication risks and interactions; assess adverse effects; handle and administer high-risk medications safely.
candidate_reasons_resolved: Rebuilt the item as four substantive heat-safety teaching statements of comparable length rather than one long correct statement against three very short distractors.
Placed the unsafe statement in a noninitial option and removed the conspicuous longest-answer pattern.
Removed the unsupported implication that a short heating-pad exposure can be considered safe; current labeling provides no such exception.
audit_note: Independent adversarial review confirms C is the only statement inconsistent with current labeling because any direct external heating-pad exposure at or around the patch is unsafe and no 15-minute exception is provided. A and B directly match §5.8/§2.7, while D is supported by §5.9. No second defensible answer or material cueing remains.
